"Punch it in!" I yell over the whistling shriek of escaping air. The atmosphere is thinning fast now; my ears pop painfully. 

Vance brace his feet against the ceiling, wedging himself into the narrow space, and hammers his four-digit override into the keypad with his left hand. The panel flashes green. I jam the butt of the heavy flashlight into the manual release lever and wrench it down. 

The access hatch pops open, revealing the cramped, dark service tube. Wedged inside at a crooked, forty-five-degree angle is the five-foot cylinder of the distress buoy, its nosecone crushed against the warped outer hull plating. *CRACK-HISS.*

I whip my head around. 

Pushing through the center of the six-inch-thick titanium airlock hatch is something that looks like a cross between a deep-sea crab claw and a shard of obsidian. It is glistening with a strange, bioluminescent ichor that boils away in the leaking atmosphere, yet the appendage itself is entirely unfazed by the cold. It wrenches sideways, and the titanium tears like wet cardboard. 

A gap the size of a dinner plate opens up. The whistle becomes a roar.

"Vance!" 

I lunge, my boots magnetized to the deck plates, and catch the webbing of his harness with one hand. The sheer force of the gale threatens to dislocate my shoulder. Behind the tearing metal of the airlock, through the swirling fog of rapid condensation, I see a cluster of pale, multifaceted eyes pressing against the gap, drinking in the blue light of our dying ship. 

I can't pull Vance back against the gale, and I can't reach the buoy's manual trigger inside the tube. 

"The flashlight!" Vance screams, his voice thin and distant in the roaring thinner air. His boots are inches from the jagged, snapping appendage. "Throw it!"

I look at the heavy, mag-clamped flashlight in my free hand. I look at the blinking red light on the nosecone of the jammed rocket, three feet inside the service access. 

If the explosive bolts blow inward, it'll shred the corridor. If they blow outward, it’ll take the whole dorsal collar with it. 

Either way, it beats getting dragged into the dark.

Holding Vance against the hurricane of escaping air with every shred of muscle I have left, I draw my arm back, aim for the crushed nosecone of the buoy, and hurl the heavy steel flashlight into the service tube like a grenade.

Time stretches, fracturing into jagged, hyper-focused milliseconds. 

The heavy steel casing of the flashlight tumbles end over end, fighting the violent crosswind of the decompressing corridor. For a horrifying fraction of a second, the gale catches it, pulling its trajectory wide—it’s going to miss the nosecone and get sucked straight into the airlock breach.

Then, the magnetic base of the flashlight snaps sideways, catching the edge of the buoy’s warped steel cradle. It pivots violently and slams dead-center into the crushed pressure sensor on the nosecone.

*Click.*

I don't wait to see the spark. I kick the manual release on my mag-boots, wrap both arms around Vance’s chest, and let the hurricane of escaping air yank us backward—not toward the breach, but curling my body so we careen hard against the heavy frame of the bridge doorway just a few feet away. I hook my elbow around the bulkhead lip and lock my boots back onto the deck plates, burying my face against Vance’s shoulder.

The world turns white.

It isn't a sound; by now the air is too thin to carry the true roar of a detonation. Instead, it is a concussive wave of pure kinetic violence that slams through the steel of the ship and hits my chest like a sledgehammer. The explosive bolts on the fairing blow, and a microsecond later, the Class-4 buoy’s solid-fuel rocket ignites inside a closed, warped tube.

A blinding jet of white-hot plasma erupts from the service access panel. 

Having nowhere to go forward, the rocket’s exhaust backfires into the companionway, instantly incinerating the remaining oxygen in a flash-fire, before the sheer, localized overpressure does the rest. The warped outer hull plating above the tube gives way entirely. 

The dorsal collar—and the airlock attached to it—doesn't just breach; it *detonates* outward into the void.

Through the strobe-light flash of fire and tearing titanium, I catch a glimpse of the nightmare in the airlock. The creature's obsidian appendage is caught directly in the path of the rocket’s misfire. The bioluminescent ichor flashes into purple steam as the plasma jet shears the limb clean off at the joint. Beyond the shredded hatch, a massive, multi-limbed silhouette is illuminated by the glare, recoiling in a silent, spasmodic frenzy as a jagged piece of the ship's hull—and the screaming, corkscrewing rocket of the distress buoy—slams directly into its bulk, tumbling it backward into the black.

The roar of the wind vanishes instantly, replaced by the eerie, absolute silence of space. The sudden loss of pressure causes my suit to balloon outward, the fabric stiffening until my joints feel like they’re encased in cured concrete. Around us, the grey fog of condensation freezes into a billion tiny diamonds, hanging suspended in the sudden stillness before drifting lazily out the gaping hole where the dorsal ceiling used to be.

For a long moment, I can’t move. My visor is spiderwebbed with frost on the inside from my own ragged breathing. My ribs feel like a bag of broken glass, the med-patch entirely overwhelmed by the fresh trauma of the blast wave. 

I force my head up. 

Where the companionway ceiling used to be, there is only a jagged, glowing-red rim of melted titanium framing a pristine view of the starfield. Drifting away into the abyss, tumbles a massive, curled shape of charred chitin, trailing frozen ribbons of glowing violet blood. Speared straight through its midsection is the distress buoy, its micro-thruster finally burning out, its strobe light blinking a steady, rhythmic white against the dark. 

*Beep... Beep... Beep...*

The signal is broadcasting directly into my helmet’s short-range comms. The buoy is active. It’s transmitting. Whatever rescue crews are in this sector, they just got a pinpoint lock on a dead monster.

I look down at my hands. They are still locked in a death-grip around Vance’s harness. 

Slowly, I pull him back through the threshold of the bridge and hit the manual override beside my knee. With a heavy, grinding *thud*, the bridge's emergency blast doors slide shut, sealing off the ruined companionway and cutting us off from the void. 

The bridge is pitch black now, save for the dim, emerald glow of our suit HUDs. There is no air left in the room. No heat. No power. 

I let go of Vance, and we both drift upward a few inches, tethered only by my magnetized boots. I tap my helmet against his, establishing a physical conduction link since our short-range radios are fried by the EMP of the blast. 

"Vance?" I croak, my voice rattling in the tiny ecosystem of my helmet. "Talk to me."

There is a long, agonizing pause. Then, a weak, static-laced chuckle vibrates through the polycarbonate of my visor. 

"I think..." Vance’s voice is paper-thin, slurred by pain and oxygen deprivation. "I think you voided the warranty on that flashlight, Skipper."

A dry, breathless laugh escapes my throat, immediately followed by a wince of agony from my chest. I check the readout on my wrist. Suit integrity: holding. Suit oxygen: forty-two minutes. 

It’s not four hours. Not anymore. If a rescue ship doesn't jump into the system on the back of that buoy's signal in the next forty minutes, we’re going to suffocate in the dark anyway. 

I reach out, find Vance’s good hand in the gloom, and squeeze the thick fabric of his glove. Looking up at the frosted, unyielding viewport of the bridge, I watch the distant, rhythmic flash of the buoy fading into the starfield, and settle in to wait.

The silence of a dead ship is a heavy thing. Without the background hum of the scrubbers, the thrum of the reactor, or the creak of the hull, the only sounds left in the universe are the wet rasp of my own lungs and the erratic, clicking purr of our suit regulators.

*Thirty-one minutes.*

The cold is the first thing to really bite. With the ship’s main power gone, the ambient temperature on the bridge is plummeting toward absolute zero. Our suits have internal heaters, of course, powered by the micro-cells in our packs, but they aren't built for long-haul exposure in a hard vacuum. I can already feel the chill seeping through the soles of my mag-boots, a creeping numbness that starts in my toes and works its way up my shins. 

Vance is drifting beside me like a balloon on a string, his boots unlatched, held down only by my grip on his harness. His breathing is too shallow. We keep our helmets pressed together, a tiny, fragile bridge of polycarbonate and bone conduction. 

"Hey," I whisper, the word fogging the inside of my visor before the defroster grid struggles to clear it. "Stay with me, Vance. Don't you dare go to sleep."

"Not sleeping," he murmurs, the vibration barely registering against my temple. "Just... resting my eyes. Hell of a light show, Skipper."

"Best fireworks in the sector." 

I shift my weight, and a white-hot lance of fire stabs through my left side. Definitely broken ribs. Maybe a punctured lung, held at bay only by the pressurized environment of the suit. The med-patch on my torso has gone entirely cold, its reservoir of synthetic adrenaline and painkillers completely spent. Every breath feels like inhaling crushed glass.

*Twenty-two minutes.*

Out beyond the frosted, armored glass of the bridge viewport, the distress buoy’s strobe is barely visible now—a tiny, dying star pulsing in the dark, still impaled in the drifting corpse of the thing that tore our ship apart. 

I find myself staring at it, hypnotized by the rhythm. *Flash. Dark. Flash. Dark.* 

My mind, starved of oxygen and swimming in endorphins, starts to wander. I think about the science vessels that are going to comb through this wreckage. I think about the company executives who will care infinitely more about the charred, violet-blooded carcass drifting out there than the crew it butchered. Did we kill the only one? Or was it just a scout? A scavenger drawn to the noise of our mining lasers? 

"Skipper?" Vance’s voice is so faint now I have to press my helmet harder against his just to hear it. 

"I'm here."

"My O2..." He coughs, a wet, rattling sound. "Took a hit in the corridor. Slow leak in the manifold, I think. I'm at... four percent."

My heart slams against my broken ribs. I pull my head back, breaking the link, and grab his wrist, pulling his HUD readout toward my visor. The emerald numbers are flashing a violent, angry red. *03%.* 

"No, no, no," I mutter, my clumsy, pressurized gloves fumbling at my own chest pack. Every deep-space EVA suit comes with a buddy-breather—an umbilical hose meant to share air in an emergency. I rip the Velcro flap open, yank the coiled steel-braided line free, and jam the nozzle into the intake port on Vance's collar. 

I twist the valve. There’s a sharp hiss as our systems equalize.

On my wrist, my own readout plummets as my tank rushes to fill his depleted one. 

*Nineteen minutes... Fifteen... Twelve...*

"What did you do?" he slurs. "You idiot. You could've made it."

I'm so cold. My fingers have stopped hurting; I can't feel Vance's harness anymore, though I know my hand is still locked around it, frozen in place by the stiffened joints of the suit.

*Flash. Dark. Flash. Dark.*

I close my eyes. The pain in my chest is fading now, replaced by a strange, floating warmth. The grey at the edges of my vision rushes inward, swallowing the red warning lights, swallowing the dark of the bridge. 

Then, the darkness turns brilliant, blinding blue. 

My eyes snap open. 

Outside the viewport, space itself seems to tear open. "Told you," I whisper to the dark, and let the blackness take me.

Miller’s expression doesn't change. He taps the screen of his slate, and turns it toward me.

It’s currently wrapped in a containment net, being winched into the massive ventral hangar of the *Vindicator*. In the heavy silence that follows, the only sound is the steady *beep... beep... beep* of my heart monitor. 

I slowly turn my head to look at Vance. He looks back at me, slowly lowers his plastic spoon into the half-eaten cup of green paste, and lets out a long, weary sigh. 

"Forget hazard pay, Skipper," Vance mutters. "I want a promotion."
